findings.title: Backup code login bypasses password verification, reducing 2FA to a single factor
findings.body: In the credentials `authorize` callback, the password is only verified inside `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` (line 121). Any request that includes a non-empty `totpCode` value skips password verification entirely, and the new branch `if (user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode)` then authenticates the user based solely on the backup code. Since requests to `/api/auth/callback/credentials` are stateless (the CSRF token is freely obtainable from `/api/auth/csrf`), an attacker can POST `email`, any dummy `totpCode`, and a valid `backupCode` and log in without knowing the account password. Backup codes are static credentials stored in downloaded text files (`cal-backup-codes.txt`), screenshots, or password managers, so a leaked backup code alone now grants full account access. Note that the new `disable.ts` endpoint does verify the password before accepting a backup code, showing the intended design. The backup-code branch should require the password to be verified as well.

findings.title: Users with Google/SAML identity providers can never log in with a backup code
findings.body: For users whose `identityProvider` is GOOGLE or SAML and who have 2FA enabled (they log in via the IdP and are then redirected to `/auth/login?totp=<jwt>` to enter a second factor), a backup-code submission has an empty `totpCode`. The guard `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode)` at line 113 (and the similar one at line 117) throws `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled`/`IncorrectEmailPassword` before the new backup-code branch at line 131 is ever reached. Additionally, the login page renders `ExternalTotpFooter` (only a Cancel button) for these users, so the "Lost access" backup-code UI isn't even offered. If such a user loses their authenticator device they have no recovery path and are permanently locked out, and a crafted request gets a misleading "account created with identity provider" error.

findings.title: "missing_backup_codes" message tells users to generate codes in settings, but no such feature exists
findings.body: The new string `missing_backup_codes` reads "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." This error is returned by both the login and disable endpoints whenever a user has 2FA enabled but `backupCodes` is null — which is the case for every user who enabled 2FA before this feature shipped, since the migration only adds a nullable column and no codes are backfilled. There is no settings UI in this PR (or elsewhere) to generate or regenerate backup codes; the only way to obtain them is to disable and re-enable 2FA. Affected users who click "Lost access" will see an instruction that leads nowhere.

findings.title: No test coverage for the core backup-code behavior (login, single-use consumption, disable)
findings.body: The PR's main feature — authenticating with a backup code, consuming it so it cannot be reused, and disabling 2FA with a backup code — has no test at all. The only test changes exercise the download/copy/close buttons on the setup screen, and the file itself adds a TODO acknowledging this ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup"), while the PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added to prove the feature works. A regression such as codes not being single-use (or being consumed but login failing) would ship undetected.

findings.title: Closing the modal without clicking "Close" leaves parent UI stale and modal state dirty
findings.body: Previously `onEnable()` was called immediately when 2FA was successfully enabled; now it is only called from the "Close" button on the backup-codes screen (line 269). If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (the dialog's X button, Escape, or overlay click, which go through `onOpenChange`), `onEnable()` never fires and `resetState()` never runs. Consequences: the parent page never learns 2FA was enabled, so the two-factor switch still shows as off even though `twoFactorEnabled` is now true in the database, and reopening the modal resumes at the stale DisplayBackupCodes step showing old codes instead of the password step. A user who then tries to enable 2FA again will hit the `two-factor-already-enabled` error.

findings.title: Backup-code consumption is a read-modify-write race
findings.body: Consuming a backup code decrypts the JSON array, finds the index, sets `backupCodes[index] = null`, and writes back the re-encrypted array in a separate `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent login requests with the same backup code can both read the array before either writes, so both succeed — the "each code can be used exactly once" guarantee (which the UI copy promises) does not hold under concurrent requests. Similarly, two concurrent logins with two different codes can clobber each other's update, resurrecting an already-consumed code. Consider atomically updating (e.g., a transaction with re-validation, or filtering the code out and updating with a condition) or at least using `splice` instead of leaving `null` entries in the stored array.

findings.title: tabIndex={-1} on PasswordField visibility toggle removes keyboard access everywhere
findings.body: Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button changes the shared `PasswordField` component, which is used across the app (login, signup, password change, 2FA setup/disable, etc.). Keyboard and assistive-technology users can no longer tab to the toggle to reveal what they typed — the button's own `sr-only` label ("Show password") suggests it was intended to be accessible. If the goal was to fix tab order in a specific 2FA form, it should be done per-instance rather than degrading accessibility for every password field in the product.
